# Part 1: Broken pipes and signals

This loop prints one line per second for 5 seconds. Time it when only its first line is wanted:

```bash
time (for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do echo "line $i"; sleep 1; done | head -n 1)
```

#TODO [the loop needs 5 seconds to finish, but the whole command takes about 1 second. What happened to the loop, and when exactly did it happen? <2pts>]
the loop ended after reading only one line, because of the head -n 1 command. once the first loop finish, it closes the pipe  between the loop and the head. so the whole loop takes 1 second due to the "sleep 1" command.
#TODO [why do you think it took slightly more than one second? <1pts>]
the extra few seconds are due to overhead time of the computer. It takes time to open the subshell of the loop, run the commands, close the pipe and send the end signal.

`yes` prints `y` forever (see `man yes`). Run:

```bash
yes | head -n 3
yes | head -n 3; echo "${PIPESTATUS[@]}"
kill -l 13
```

`$?` only gives you the exit status of the *last* command in a pipe; the bash variable `PIPESTATUS` holds the exit status of every command in the pipe.

#TODO [why does `yes | head -n 3` finish at all, if `yes` never stops on its own? <1pts>] 
the "yes loop" tries to enter the forth loop but the command "head -n 3" stops it , with the SIGPIPE from the operating system.
#TODO [what are the two exit statuses, and what does `kill -l 13` tell you about the first one? (An exit status above 128 means "killed by signal number status − 128".) <1pts>] 
Since I am working on a Mac (using zsh), I had to use the lowercase variable pipestatus instead of PIPESTATUS. The two exit statuses are 141 (for the yes command) and 0 (for the head command). The command kill -l 13 outputs PIPE, which tells us that the first process was killed by signal 13 (broken pipe).

#TODO [**without running it**: what would `yes | sort | head -n 3` do, and why? <1pts>]
the command will forever run without printing anything.  sort has to read all the input before it sorts it and passing it to head. because 'yes' keeps giving input, 'sort'
 will never be able to finish the operation.

#TODO [what does `tee` do, and where does the output of each command go? <1pts>]
'tee' takes the data, and splits it in two. It takes one copy and saves it into a file - tx_oh.csv.
It takes the original data flow and passes it further along the chain to the next command (in our case, to the 'wc -l' command, which counts the lines).
#TODO [how would you use `tee` to also keep a copy of the unfiltered header line? <1pts>]
I would first run head -n 1 covid.csv | tee tx_oh.csv to extract the unfiltered header, save it to the file, and pass it to the screen.
#TODO [what does `tee -a` do and when would you use it? <1pts>]
The -a flag stands for 'append'. tee -a appends the output to the end of the file instead of overwriting it. I would use it if I want to add new data to an existing file without erasing its previous contents for example, to append the filtered rows to tx_oh.csv after the header was already saved there.

# Part 3: Hundreds of files

Real data often comes as hundreds or thousands of small files (one per day, per sensor, per user) rather than one big file. In this part you make such a folder yourself and then work with it using one-liners.

::: {.callout-warning}
## WSL users
Creating many files under `/mnt/c/...` (the Windows side of the disk) is very slow. Make sure your repository, and so your scratch folder, is under your Linux home (`pwd` should start with `/home/`).
:::

Split `covid.csv` into one file per day:

```bash
cd $my_52002_repo/labs/02/scratch
mkdir days
awk -F, 'NR>1 {print > ("days/" $1 ".csv")}' covid.csv
```

Inside `awk`, `print > name` writes the current line to the file called `name` (creating it the first time). Here the name is built from the first column, the date. (Mac users: if this stops with an error about too many open files, use `awk -F, 'NR>1 { if ($1 != d) { close(f); d = $1; f = "days/" d ".csv" } print > f }' covid.csv` instead, which closes each file before opening the next one.)

NR is Number of Records. the condition tells it to skip the first line (the header), without it awk would create a fie named date.csv containing only the header line.

Find the biggest file in two ways: by size in bytes, and by number of rows.

```bash
#TODO [command: the biggest file in bytes (use `ls`) <1pts>] 2020-12-31.csv.
#TODO [command: the file with the most rows (use `wc -l`, `sort` and `tail`) <1pts>]  3248 days/2020-10-18.csv
```

#TODO [the two answers are different days. Look at a few lines of each file: why is the biggest file not the one with the most rows? <2pts>] 
The file with the most bytes is 2020-12-31.csv, while the file with the most rows is 2020-10-18. This is because file size in bytes depends on the total number of characters. By December 31, the cumulative numbers of cases and deaths were much larger, meaning they required more digits (characters) to write. Therefore, each row became longer and took up more bytes, making the overall file larger even if it had slightly fewer rows.

On which day does Wyoming first appear in the data? Use `grep -l` (read `man grep`) together with `head`, in one line.

```bash
#TODO [command <1pts>] grep -l "Wyoming" days/*.csv | head -n 1
```

#TODO [the day <1pts>] days/2020-03-11.csv
#TODO [`grep` looked at the files in the order of their names. Why is that order the same as the order of the dates here? Would it still be true for files named like `3-11-2020.csv`? <2pts>] 
The filenames use the YYYY-MM-DD format, which places the most significant time unit first (year, then month, then day) and uses leading zeros for single-digit months and days. Because of this, standard alphabetical sorting matches the chronological order. It would not be true for files named like 3-11-2020.csv, because alphabetical sorting compares character by character from left to right.

Every file in `days` is missing the header line. Write a `for` loop that puts the header line of `covid.csv` at the top of every file. Hint: `{ cmd1; cmd2; } > out` sends the output of both commands into `out`. Then check your work with `grep -l` and `wc -l`.

#TODO [why can't you write `cat header.csv "$f" > "$f"` in the loop? (Remember `p2.txt` from Lab 1.) <1pts>]
Because the `>` operator immediately empties (erases) the file "$f" before the `cat` command even starts reading it, so all the data inside "$f" would be lost.

Rename every file from `2020-MM-DD.csv` to `MM-DD.csv`. A classic one-liner trick is to let `sed` *write* the commands and only then hand them to `bash`. First look at the commands without running them:

```bash
cd days
ls | sed 's/^2020-\(.*\)$/mv 2020-\1 \1/' | head -n 3
```

```
[output <1pts>]
mv 2020-01-21.csv 01-21.csv
mv 2020-01-22.csv 01-22.csv
mv 2020-01-23.csv 01-23.csv
```

When the commands look right, run them all by replacing `| head -n 3` with `| bash`, then `cd ..`.

#TODO [what do `\(...\)` and `\1` do in the `sed` pattern? (See `man sed`.) <1pts>]
... captures and saves the matched part of the text (everything after 2020, which is MM.DD), and ֿֿ\1 pastes that saved text back into the replacement string.
#TODO [why is it a good habit to look at the generated commands before piping them into `bash`? <1pts>]
Because a small mistake in the `sed` pattern could generate wrong 'mv' commands that accidentally overwrite or ruin hundreds of files at once. Checking the output first ensures the commands are safe before executing them.
File names with spaces break many one-liners. Try:

```bash
touch "days/my notes.txt"
for f in $(ls days/*.txt); do echo "[$f]"; done
for f in days/*.txt; do echo "[$f]"; done
rm "days/my notes.txt"
```

```
[output of the two loops <1pts>]
[days/my]
[notes.txt]
[days/my notes.txt]
```

#TODO [why does the first loop see two files? <2pts>]
Because the shell splits the unquoted output of $(ls ...) by spaces (word splitting). Since "my notes.txt" has a space in the middle, the loop treats days/my and notes.txt as two separate items.

Finally, compress the files, first one at a time and then in parallel. `xargs -n 10` hands the file names to `gzip` ten at a time, and `-P 4` runs up to four `gzip`s at the same time (read `man xargs`):

```bash
nproc
cp -r days g1
cp -r days g4
time (ls g1/*.csv | xargs gzip)
time (ls g4/*.csv | xargs -n 10 -P 4 gzip)
du -sh days g1
tar czf days.tar.gz days
ls -lh days.tar.gz
```

```
[output <1pts>] 
zsh: command not found: nproc
( ls g1/*.csv | xargs gzip; )  1.45s user 0.37s system 94% cpu 1.925 total
( ls g4/*.csv | xargs -n 10 -P 4 gzip; )  1.72s user 0.62s system 348% cpu 0.670 total
 35M    days
9.7M    g1
-rw-r--r--@ 1 elivolowelsky  staff   9.0M Oct 29 19:43 days.tar.gz
```

#TODO [how many times faster was the parallel version? Why is it not exactly 4 times faster? <2pts>]
The parallel version was about 2.87 times faster (1.925s / 0.670s ≈ 2.87). It is not exactly 4 times faster because of the overhead of starting and managing multiple processes, and because all 4 processes compete for disk I/O (reading and writing files to the disk at the same time). also: on macOS, nproc is not available.
#TODO [`days.tar.gz` is smaller than the folder of separately gzipped files. Why? (Hint: what can `gzip` take advantage of when all the files are compressed as one stream?) <2pts>]
When compressing all files together as one continuous stream (days.tar.gz), 'gzip' can exploit redundancies (repeated text like state and county names, headers, and date prefixes) across different files, and it only writes one gzip file header/footer instead of 346 separate ones.

# Part 4: When there are too many files

## The argument list

Make a folder with 200,000 empty files (this takes a few seconds):

```bash
cd $my_52002_repo/labs/02/scratch
mkdir lots && cd lots
seq -w 1 200000 | sed 's/$/.txt/' | xargs touch
ls | wc -l
ls *.txt | wc -l
rm *.txt
getconf ARG_MAX
```

```
[output <1pts>]
 200000
zsh: argument list too long: ls
       0
zsh: argument list too long: rm
1048576
```

#TODO [why do `ls *.txt` and `rm *.txt` fail, when `ls | wc -l` works fine? Who expands the `*`, and what is `ARG_MAX`? <2pts>]
The shell itself expands the '*' before running the command, turning *.txt into a massive list of 200,000 filenames. This exceeds ARG_MAX (the maximum total length in bytes of arguments that can be passed to a single command), causing an "Argument list too long" error. Also, ls | wc -l works fine because no arguments are passed to 'ls', it reads the directory directly and sends the output through a pipe, which has no size limit.
#TODO [`xargs touch` created all 200,000 files without this error. How? (See `man xargs`.) <1pts>]
xargs reads the filenames from standard input and splits them into smaller batches that fit within the system's ARG_MAX limit, running touch multiple times instead of all at once.
Now delete them correctly, and remove the folder:

```bash
#TODO [one command that deletes all the files in `lots` using `find` and `xargs` <1pts>] find . -type f | xargs rm
cd .. && rmdir lots
```

## Running out of inodes

Every file and folder uses one *inode* (you met inode numbers with `ls -i` in Lab 1). A disk has a fixed number of inodes, decided when it was formatted, so it can run out of inodes while it still has lots of free space.

```bash
df -h ~
df -i ~
```

```
[output <1pts>]
Filesystem      Size    Used   Avail Capacity iused ifree %iused  Mounted on
/dev/disk1s2   932Gi    42Gi   872Gi     5%    559k  9.1G    0%   /System/Volumes/Data
Filesystem   512-blocks      Used  Available Capacity iused      ifree %iused  Mounted on
/dev/disk1s2 1953595632  88194856 1827916064     5%  558779 9139580320    0%   /System/Volumes/Data
```

#TODO [how many more files could you create on your home disk before you run out of inodes? <1pts>]
According to the ifree column in df -i ~, I can create billions more files ,about 9.1 billion, because macOS dynamically allocates inodes as needed.

Your real disk has far too many inodes to use up, so build a tiny disk inside a file and fill that one instead. This needs `sudo`. (Mac users: macOS's file system creates inodes as needed, so this cannot be reproduced on a Mac. Do it on a Linux machine, e.g. the remote machine from Lecture 2.)

```bash
cd $my_52002_repo/labs/02/scratch
truncate -s 20M tiny.img             # a 20 MB empty file
mkfs.ext4 -q -N 1000 tiny.img         # format it as a disk with about 1,000 inodes
mkdir tiny
sudo mount -o loop tiny.img tiny      # use the file as a disk, at the folder tiny
sudo chown $USER tiny
df -h tiny
df -i tiny
cd tiny
seq 1 2000 | sed 's/$/.txt/' | xargs touch
ls | wc -l
df -h .
df -i .
echo "hello" >> 1.txt
mkdir newdir
```

```
[output <1pts>]

touch: cannot touch '2000.txt': No space left on device
998
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on

Filesystem     Inodes IUsed IFree IUse% Mounted on
/dev/loop0       1008  1008     0  100% /tmp/tiny
mkdir: cannot create directory 'newdir': No space left on device
root@b9b02aa91c9f:/tmp/tiny# ls | wc -l
df -h .
df -i .
echo "hello" >> 1.txt
mkdir newdir
998
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/loop0       16M   48K   15M   1% /tmp/tiny

/dev/loop0       1008  1008     0  100% /tmp/tiny
mkdir: cannot create directory 'newdir': No space left on device
root@b9b02aa91c9f:/tmp/tiny#
```

#TODO [how many files did you manage to create, and what was the error? <1pts>]

#TODO [what do `df -h .` and `df -i .` say about space and inodes at that point? <1pts>]
df -h shows the disc is almost empty, only 1% is used and more than 15MB available.
df -i shows all the inodes are used -100 % and 0% available, it means that the inodes were finished before the space was finished, thats why there is no option to create new files.
#TODO [why did appending to `1.txt` work, but `mkdir newdir` fail? <2pts>]
adding text to 1.txt worked because the file already exists and has its own inode.
The operation only needs a little disk space for the new content, and there is plenty of free space. mkdir newdir failed because creating a new directory requires a new inode, and all the inodes are in use. So you can add content to existing files, but you cannot create new files or directories, even though the disk is almost empty.
#TODO [a server's disk shows "No space left on device" but `df -h` says it is only 30% full. What would you check, and what kind of program might have caused it? <2pts>]
I would run df -i to check if the inodes are fully used (IUse close to 100%). If so, I would check which filed contains the most files. The problem is usually caused from a program that creates a big number of small files and doesnt delete them.
Clean up:

```bash
cd ..
sudo umount tiny
rmdir tiny
rm tiny.img
```
